summary: Proposes a distributed name service for the DARPA Internet, to focus discussion in hope of eventual standards. It is a discussion proposal, not a specification.

eli5.summary: Instead of one list of names kept in one place, this memo suggests spreading the job across many computers.

questions: what is the distributed system for internet name service
how does hierarchical domain naming work
what is the precursor to dns
subtitle: An early proposal for a distributed name service architecture for the Internet.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET naming convention (user@host) needed to be generalized for the emerging Internet, which would span multiple interconnected networks with many organizations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 830 proposes a distributed system with Domain Name Servers (DNSs) organized in a hierarchy, where domains are administrative entities. Name resolution proceeds right-to-left through the hierarchy, and an Application Interface Process (AIP) layer handles service negotiation to ensure compatibility between endpoints.
tldr.outcome: This was a discussion document meant to focus discussion toward eventual standards. It influenced the development of what became the Domain Name System (DNS), though the final DNS design (RFC 1035) took a different technical approach.

facts.label: Components
facts.value: Endpoint DNS, Intermediate DNS, Application Interface Processes

facts.label: Recommended transport
facts.value: UDP (over TCP to avoid connection overhead)

today: This RFC is a discussion proposal that preceded the development of what became the Domain Name System (DNS, RFC 1035). While it did not become the standard, it influenced thinking about distributed name services and hierarchical domain structures. The final DNS design took a different technical approach but adopted many of the same architectural principles.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 830 proposes an architecture for a distributed System for Internet Name Service (SINS). The document's stated purpose is to focus discussion on distributed naming for the Internet in hopes of reaching eventual consensus on standards.

The ARPANET had used the naming convention <user>@<host> for many years, but this scheme needed to be generalized to support internetworking across multiple administrative organizations. A hierarchical Internet Naming Convention was proposed, with names like <user>@<domain>.<domain>...<domain>, where domains are hierarchically related administrative entities.
sections.eli5: This is a proposal for how computers on the Internet could have names, and how to look them up when you want to send a message to one.

sections.title: System Architecture
sections.content:
The SINS system consists of two layers:

  • Domain Name Service (DNS): An application-independent network service for resolving domain names. Each domain has an associated Domain Name Server (DNS). Domains are administrative entities, not necessarily topological ones.
  • Application Interface (AIP): Isolates application processes from the domain name service, allowing the same naming service to be shared among various user applications like SMTP, FTP, and Telnet.

For operational efficiency, the AIP is assumed to be combined with its associated DNS to form an endpoint DNS at each domain. Intermediate DNS servers (without associated application processes) simply resolve first-generation subdomains.

Each endpoint domain maintains a database of name-to-address correspondences for top-level domains. Intermediate domains maintain databases of their own subdomains. The disjoint nature of intermediate databases allows local updates without global standardization.
sections.eli5: Each domain (like a company or university) has a name server that knows where to find local computers. The name servers talk to each other to find computers in other domains.

sections.title: Domain Name Resolution
sections.content:
When a source application requests to contact a destination, the local AIP presents the fully qualified domain name (like TSC.SRI.ARPA) to its co-located DNS for resolution.

DNSs resolve the domain name by working right-to-left through the hierarchy. The source endpoint DNS resolves the right-most simple name (the top-level domain) into the address of that domain's DNS. It then acts as a hub, polling that DNS and subsequent intermediate DNSs with requests for further resolution, progressively moving left through the remaining domain names.

Each DNS in the chain resolves the next domain name to the left. An intermediate DNS may choose to return the resulting address to the source DNS or forward the request to the next DNS. This hop-by-hop resolution eventually reaches the destination endpoint DNS, whose address is returned to the source.
sections.eli5: To find a computer in another domain, you ask your local nameserver. It asks the top-level domain's nameserver, which asks the next domain down the line, and so on until it finds the right domain, then sends the answer back.

sections.title: Service Negotiation
sections.content:
Beyond domain name resolution to a network address, applications often need further negotiation to ensure compatibility. RFC 830 calls this what-can-you-do-for-me negotiation.

The Application Interface Processes negotiate the availability and compatibility of both transport services (like TCP or UDP) and application services (like SMTP, FTP, or NIFTP for mail and file transfer). This negotiation is necessary because a source might request NIFTP service while the destination only offers FTP. The negotiation mechanism allows the source and destination to discover compatible services and establish communication using the best available option.

This two-stage process—first resolving the domain name to find the destination's DNS, then negotiating which services are compatible—allows dynamic binding and flexibility in system design.
sections.eli5: After finding the right computer, you ask it what services it offers. If it does not offer what you want, it tells you what it does offer instead.

sections.title: Name Service Protocols
sections.content:
RFC 830 defines a uniform command-based protocol for communication among the three main component pairs: Application Process/AIP, AIP/DNS, and DNS/DNS.

Each command begins with a command type octet and the number of items, followed by a variable number of items. Each item has a type indicator, a content length, and the content itself. Item types include service (transport/application protocol), name (domain name), address (network address), and optional comment.

Commands follow a request-response pattern:

  • Request: The source specifies a service type and destination name.
  • Affirmative Response: The destination offers the requested service and provides the address or next-level domain name.
  • Negative Response: The requested service is not available, or the domain cannot be resolved.
  • Incompatible Service Response: The exact service is unavailable, but an alternative compatible service is offered.

The RFC recommends UDP for transport because it offers sufficient capacity for most commands and avoids the overhead of TCP connection establishment.
sections.eli5: Messages between nameservers follow a standard format: a request for a name, and a response with either the address, an alternative service, or an error message.
